taxonomy.subtopic: Reduced delayed rectifier potassium current and prolonged repolarization

questions.stem_html:
A 14-year-old girl collapses while swimming and spontaneously regains consciousness. Her mother has had unexplained syncope, and a maternal cousin died suddenly at age 18. ECG shows a corrected QT interval of 520 ms. Genetic testing identifies a loss-of-function variant in KCNQ1.

Which action-potential change results from this mutation?

options.text_html: Increased funny-current influx accelerates phase 4 depolarization
Reduced outward potassium current during phase 3 prolongs ventricular repolarization
Reduced fast sodium influx slows phase 0 in atrial tissue only
Increased L-type calcium-channel inactivation shortens the plateau
Increased inward rectifier potassium current delays depolarization

questions.explanation_html: KCNQ1 contributes to the slow delayed rectifier potassium current. Loss of function reduces phase-3 outward current, prolonging the action potential and enabling early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes. The exercise-triggered phenotype and KCNQ1 mutation identify LQT1 due to deficient repolarizing potassium current.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Funny current affects pacemaker automaticity and does not directly explain prolonged ventricular QT.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: A sodium-channel conduction defect may widen QRS or cause Brugada phenotypes, but KCNQ1 specifically affects repolarizing potassium current.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Faster calcium inactivation would tend to shorten, not prolong, ventricular action potentials.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Increased outward potassium current would generally abbreviate repolarization rather than prolong QT.

questions.educational_objective: Explain congenital long QT syndrome through reduced phase-3 potassium current, prolonged repolarization, early afterdepolarizations, and torsades risk.
